title: 🐍 Exercise 1: Variables and Data Types 🧩
concept: In Python, variables store values of different data types (integers, strings, etc.). Concatenation requires compatible types: you can't directly add numbers to text. Use `str()` to convert numbers to strings. Variables must be defined before use. Assignment (=) stores values in variables.
description: Fix the code so it correctly assigns the value to the variable and prints it. 🔍
codeOkForExpect:
numero = 10
texto = 'is a number'
print(str(numero) + ' ' + texto)  # ✅
successMessage: 🎉 Well done! Now the code correctly prints the concatenation. 🐍✨

title: 🔄 Exercise 2: Conditional Statements ⚖️
concept: Conditional structures (if/elif/else) evaluate boolean expressions to decide which code to execute. Indentation is crucial in Python to define code blocks. Each condition must have a clear expression (e.g., num > 0). Only one block executes, depending on the first true condition.
description: Fix the code so it correctly evaluates whether a number is positive, negative, or zero. 🔄
successMessage: ✅ Correct! You have mastered indentation in Python. 🎯

title: 🔁 Exercise 3: 'for' Loops and Lists 📋
concept: `for` loops iterate over elements of a list or iterable. In each iteration, a temporary variable (e.g., 'i') takes a value from the list. The `print()` function requires parentheses in Python 3. Indentation defines which code repeats in the loop.
description: Fix the code so it prints each element of the list correctly. 🔄
successMessage: 🎯 Well done! Now the loop works like a Swiss clock. ⏱️🐍

title: 📦 Exercise 4: Functions �
concept: Functions are defined with `def` and can take parameters. `return` sends a value back to the caller, while `print()` only displays text. To use a function's result, you must return it. Functions without `return` default to `None`.
description: Fix the code so that the function correctly returns the sum of two numbers. ➕
codeOkForExpect:
def sumar(a, b):
    return a + b  # 🔙
resultado = sumar(3, 4)
print(resultado)
errorSimulation: ❌ Error: The function does not return a value. 🚪
successMessage: ✨ Well done! Now the function correctly returns values. 💻

title: 📖 Exercise 5: Dictionaries 🔑
concept: Dictionaries store key-value pairs. Keys must be immutable (strings, numbers) and enclosed in quotes. Access values with `dictionary[key]`. Dictionaries use {} and are mutable. Keys must exist to avoid KeyError.
description: Fix the code to correctly access dictionary values. 🔍
successMessage: 🎉 Well done! Now the dictionary is an open book. 📘✨

title: 📝 Exercise 6: Lists and Methods 🧩
concept: Lists are ordered, mutable collections. The `+` operator creates new lists, while `append()` modifies the original. List methods (like append) perform in-place actions. To modify existing lists, use methods instead of operators.
description: Fix the code to correctly add an element to the list. ➕
errorSimulation: ❌ Error: The list is not modified correctly. 🚫
successMessage: ✅ Well done! Now you master list methods. 🐍🎯

title: 🛡️ Exercise 7: Exception Handling ⚠️
concept: Exception handling (try/except) prevents errors from crashing the program. Specific error types (e.g., ZeroDivisionError) can be caught. The `try` block contains risky code; `except` handles errors. Clear error messages are good practice.
description: Fix the code to properly handle a division by zero exception. 🔄
expectedConsoleOutput: Error: Division by zero is not allowed.
successMessage: 🛡️ Correct! Now your code is error-proof. 💪

title: 👥 Exercise 8: Classes and Objects 🏗️
concept: Classes are blueprints for objects. The `__init__` method initializes object attributes using `self`. Instance variables require `self.` to persist. Access attributes with `object.attribute`. Instantiation is done by calling the class.
description: Fix the code to correctly define and instantiate a class. 🔧
errorSimulation: ❌ Error: The attribute 'nombre' is not correctly assigned. 🚫
successMessage: 🎓 Well done! Now OOP has no secrets for you. 🐍✨

title: λ Exercise 9: Functional Programming 🎯
concept: Lambda functions are anonymous one-line functions. Defined with `lambda parameters: expression`. Useful for simple operations. In Python 3, `print()` requires parentheses. Lambdas can be assigned to variables for reuse.
description: Fix the code to correctly use a lambda function. ➡️
codeKoToRefactor:
doble = lambda x: x * 2
print doble(5)
successMessage: ⚡ Well done! Lambdas are your new allies. 🎯

title: 📚 Exercise 10: Modules and Libraries 🌐
concept: Modules are files with reusable code. Imported with `import module`. Functions are accessed via `module.function()`. Correct syntax includes parentheses in function calls. The standard library (e.g., math) provides advanced features.
description: Fix the code to correctly import a module and use it. 🔄
errorSimulation: ❌ Error: Missing parenthesis in function call. 🧩
successMessage: 🎉 Correct! Now you master modules like an expert. 🐍🚀
